passage: In the college library's discussion room, Uma had the project tracker open on her laptop. Four names, twelve tasks. "Ritvik gets nothing this time," she said. Jaya looked up. "Nothing? He's in the group." "He sent the literature review a day late in week two. I had to stay up formatting everything. I'm not risking the final report on him." "He had fever that week, remember?" "Still." Uma left his row empty and split his tasks between herself and Jaya. When Ritvik messaged offering to do the survey charts, she replied, "Covered, thanks." Later, alone in the room, she noticed that the charts he'd made for the midterm were the neatest in the whole file. She scrolled past them quickly.

passage:
I'm Ishita, and I shared a project group with Aditi and two others this semester. In week two, Karthik submitted his part of the market survey a day late. He said sorry in the group chat. Aditi didn't reply.
At the next meeting she divided the tasks on the whiteboard. Karthik's name had nothing beside it. "It's fine, I'll do the analysis myself," she said. "We can't risk another delay." When Karthik offered to draft the slides, she said she'd already started them.
By week six he'd stopped offering. At the final review, the professor asked him a question about the survey and he answered it better than any of us. Aditi looked surprised.
I don't know what was going on in her mind. From where I sat, it looked like that one late day had become the whole story of Karthik for her.

qa.q: What did Karthik submit a day late in week two?
qa.a: He submitted his part of the market survey a day late.

qa.q: Why might giving Karthik nothing have felt sensible to Aditi?
qa.a: She was worried about another delay hurting the project, so after one late submission it felt safer to take his work herself than to trust him again.

qa.q: What went wrong in the group, and what could have fixed it?
qa.a: One late day made Aditi stop giving Karthik any tasks, and he stopped offering; giving him a small task with a clear deadline would have let the group see what he could actually do.

qa.q: How might Karthik have experienced weeks two to six?
qa.a: Karthik probably felt pushed out after apologising, which may explain why he stopped offering, even though he understood the survey better than anyone.

grounding: Told by a groupmate, it shows a student writing off a group member after one late submission and taking all tasks from him.

Monday. The design brief was due at noon, and Jomon's part came in at 4 p.m. Avni read it on the hostel stairs and texted the group: "Great. Now we look careless." Jomon's reply, "sorry, bus broke down," she left unread.
Thursday. At the planning meeting in the library, Avni wrote out the next tasks. Research: Avni. Sketches: Avni and Bina. Presentation: Bina. Jomon, sitting at the end of the table, asked, "What should I take?" Avni said, "Just review it when it's done." He closed his laptop.
Two weeks later. The group presented to their tutor. Avni had slept four hours. Jomon sat in the back row of the studio with nothing on the slides carrying his name. When the tutor asked who had done the costing, nobody had, and Avni realised it had once been on Jomon's list.

qa.q: What could Avni have done at the Thursday meeting instead?
qa.a: She could have heard his reason and given Jomon a clear task with an early check-in, instead of letting one late part decide that he got no work at all.

qa.a: For Jomon it seems he was shut out after one late day, sitting in the back with nothing carrying his name, and the costing that had been his task never got done.

passage: In the college robotics lab, the club had three weeks to build a line-following robot. In week one, Ramesh submitted the wiring diagram a day late. Samir, the team lead, sighed loudly in front of everyone. After that, he gave Ramesh nothing but cable-cutting. When Ramesh suggested a better sensor layout, Samir waved him off. "Let's stick to what works." The robot kept veering off the line. At 11 p.m. on the last night, with the lab assistant waiting to lock up, Samir was out of ideas. Ramesh quietly moved two sensors, the same layout he had suggested in week two. The robot followed the line perfectly. Samir looked at the sensors, then at Ramesh. "Why was your diagram late, that first week?" "My grandmother was in hospital," Ramesh said.

qa.q: What did Ramesh do on the last night?
qa.a: He moved two sensors, the same layout he had suggested in week two.

qa.q: Why did Samir wave off Ramesh's sensor idea?
qa.a: He felt doubtful and a bit dismissive of Ramesh after one late diagram, so the idea didn't seem worth hearing.

qa.q: What went wrong in how Samir treated Ramesh, and what could fix it?
qa.a: He let one late diagram define Ramesh; asking why it was late and judging each idea on its merits would fix it.

qa.q: What was the project like for Ramesh?
qa.a: Ramesh was stuck cutting cables while his grandmother was ill and his good idea was ignored, which must have felt lonely and unfair.

grounding: A team lead decides a member is useless after one late diagram and ignores his idea until the last night.

passage: Mehak beta, you say your project partner is hopeless because he missed one deadline? Let me tell you about my engineering days in Roorkee. Our surveying group had four boys. The group project was due in three days, and the hostel internet had been down since morning. Noor was stressed.

Tenzin had been late with his part last week, by a whole day. Since then, Noor hadn't given him anything new to do. "He's useless," she told the others. "I'll do his section myself."

Tenzin shrugged. "My grandfather was sick that week. I should have told you."

Noor felt her face go hot. She handed him the next section to do.

passage: During the Diwali break of second year, our group had a design report due, and Kamal sent his section six hours late. I remember sitting on my aunt's terrace with firecrackers going off below, furious, rewriting the introduction so his part would fit. After that I simply stopped giving Kamal anything important. When we planned the final prototype, I gave him the job of buying stationery. When he offered to do the circuit testing, I said, "It's fine, I'll handle it." One late file had become everything I thought about him. I'm Anand, and I'm still a bit embarrassed about that semester.
